Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages

Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages

开发工具 作者 armcat 热度 1004 回复 377 2026/11/15 01:43
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • Lovable: Many Apps Built on the Platform Expose Sensitive DataAI makes it easier to build your own web applications, but handling sensitive data still requires special care. We examined 159,041 Lovable projects and found many cases where personal and confidential information was accessible without logging in.Diesen Artikel auf Deutsch lesenAbout LovableLovable is a Swedish AI startup founded in Stockholm in 2023 by Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin. The platform turns plain-language descriptions into web applications and is designed to be accessible even to people with little or no programming experience.Lovable grew out of Osika’s open-source project “GPT Engineer”, released in 2023. The project evolved into the GPT Engineer App before being renamed Lovable in late 2024 and launching publicly that November.Visit the Lovable websiteThe PromiseLovable can build impressively sophisticated web projects with AI, from static websites to full applications with user management and database connections. But as soon as an application handles confidential information, one question becomes crucial: Is that data protected against unauthorized access?In its marketing, Lovable repeatedly emphasizes that no technical knowledge is needed to build projects. This can give the impression that the platform takes care of security too. Yet Lovable’s Terms & Conditions place responsibility for applications and data handling on the customers themselves.That leaves a troubling gap between the promise of an easy-to-use, all-in-one service and the responsibilities customers are expected to take on.Against this backdrop, we investigated how well sensitive data in Lovable applications is protected, in collaboration with Handelsblatt. Lina Knees reported on the findings on November 2, 2026 (in German).Research QuestionWe wanted to find out whether sensitive data in Lovable applications was accessible without logging in. We looked separately at data sent when a website first loaded and additional content we checked by making further read-only requests with the same API key.The result: We found many clear examples of sensitive data left unprotected.MethodologyWe focused on the database service Supabase. Its integration is relatively easy to analyze, and we believe it is the most widely used database service among Lovable projects. Lovable’s own database features, introduced in late 2025, are still less widely used. Similar misconfigurations may occur there too, but we did not examine them in this analysis.Using datasets from the open web archive Common Crawl, we identified and analyzed 159,041 Lovable projects from December 2025 to September 2026. Of these, 34,545 used Supabase.24,664 websites sent database records from Supabase as soon as they loaded, without requiring a login or any other interaction. That alone is not a security issue: the data may be intended for public display. But by making additional read-only requests, we were able to retrieve more database content. We found records containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of the 24,664 websites (30%).LimitationsEmail addresses can help identify records containing personal data, but they may also be public contact addresses or test data. At the same time, this approach misses personal records that contain no email address. These effects partly offset one another, though we could not establish to what extent. The 30% figure should therefore not be read as a confirmed data leak rate. It applies only to the 24,664 websites we examined more closely. Our sample, drawn from Common Crawl, is also not representative of all Lovable applications.We retrieved only parts of the datasets rather than downloading them in full. The figures below reflect the records we actually downloaded; the affected datasets may contain more. We are not publishing details of how to access them, as doing so could make further access easier.Data LeaksWe found many serious cases of exposed data, including:A German lifestyle forum exposed more than 80,000 profiles containing full names, email addresses, dates of birth, and gender information. More than 200,000 chat messages were also accessible.Several event organizers and restaurants exposed tens of thousands of records relating to ticket and food sales, with no login required. The records we inspected included email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, payment information, and ticket codes.A property management company exposed AI-generated summaries of internal emails containing sensitive information about tenants, property owners, and business partners.In a particularly serious case, a service provider exposed more than 1,000 records containing identity document details, including passport numbers, expiration dates, and nationalities. These highly sensitive identity details could be used for identity theft.Other accessible content included tens of thousands of contracts, invoices, personal photo albums, and internal WhatsApp communications.We also found numerous newsletter subscriptions, waiting lists, and contact and support inquiries. In one case, 280,000 emails sent to a provider’s customers were accessible.Depending on what it contains, exposed data like this could be used for phishing, ticket fraud, or identity theft. We could not establish whether any of it had been misused.Handelsblatt contacted Lovable with the findings of our investigation.ImplicationsOur analysis shows that many Lovable applications leave even highly sensitive data unprotected, with potentially serious consequences for the people affected.Access control mistakes can happen in any application, whether written by people or built with AI. With Lovable, database integrations follow recurring patterns, making it easier for attackers to look for similar misconfigurations across many applications. An approach that works against one app may then work against others with little extra effort. Users without a technical background also face a harder task spotting and preventing these flaws.An easy-to-use development platform does not remove the need for an expert review of access permissions before an application handles confidential data.Automated checks are no substitute for a professional security assessment.Before an application handles real customer or business data, its access permissions, interfaces, and separation between user accounts should be reviewed. These checks should be repeated after significant changes. If the necessary expertise is not available in-house, bring in qualified support.If you would like help securing your application, please get in touch.Note: This research report presents a more recent analysis and updated figures compared with the Handelsblatt article published on November 2, 2026.Get in touch for an informal conversation. We'll look at your current situation and work with you to find the right solutions.Contact an expert

What isn’t mentioned in the analysis is that we ran a System 1 decision model on each dataset to determine whether it contained privacy-sensitive data. Using a confidence threshold of 85%, we found that nearly 4,000 websites leaked such information.

Edit: That's 15,9% of all Lovable websites that use Supabase.

jacquesm 2026/11/15 05:45
That's a good question. But it is a very fine line between being a white hat that reports a vulnerability in good faith and someone who actually exploits that vulnerability and turns a vulnerability report into an actual breach. This is - in my opinion, clearly the HN hive mind disagrees - across that line.

For instance, if I run into a server and I see 'passport.jpg' in a directory listing I could download it to see if it really is a passport. But at that point in time I am flirting with becoming a defendant in a data breach rather than that I'm reporting a possible vulnerability. Sure, you could argue that the site owner might close the hole and then they could downplay that it really was a passport photograph. But I care more about the hole being closed than that I care about the contents of the file, which clearly are not meant to be disclosed based on the filename alone.

Independent researchers that are under contract with the companies they review sometimes have more leeway in what they are allowed to do. But downloading enough data to be able to run statistical analysis using LLMs is turning this into a reportable breach and that is a great way to get this whole thing to backfire, possibly to the point where the OP turns defendant.

makmanalp 2026/11/15 06:03
One thought might be - did they

the article mentions "we retrieved only parts of the datasets rather than downloading them in full", so a charitable interpretation might be that for each identified source candidate, they spot checked (or had a model spot check) a few individual records to have incontrovertible proof of breach of privacy, and then ran an aggregate count query to gauge the extent of breach. I think that would be fairly in line with "white hat" behavior that's doing the smallest amount of extra work towards a solid proof and clearly not taking the obvious and easy next step of downloading the remainder that would be required for self enrichment. Difficult to argue that there is an intention of malice.

A bad actor would be downloading /all/ the data and disclosing it to no one, and selling it while obscuring the source.

That said I agree that that certainly might fall afoul of the letter of whatever local laws apply, and certainly prosecutors can also be over-zealous in their interpretations. So personally I would never risk doing something that comes up against that line, from a personal risk POV. But idk if it's fair to argue that this is NOT good faith.

jacquesm 2026/11/15 07:00
Under an NDA you might be allowed to download bulk data and use it to see if you can get further into the system.

Companies respond in different ways to disclosures, by independent researchers and by people under contract. You are absolutely right that in many cases the findings end up in a drawer. This is a real pity. Invariably those will sooner or later be exploited by the bad guys and then the company has a serious problem: they will have to show their homework and if it is found that - at least in Europe - they were aware of the issue but did not take action it may well have the effect of changing a warning into a fine and a fine into a larger one.
